uni-nursing-community-family.title: B.Sc Nursing · Community, Maternal & Child, Mental Health
uni-nursing-community-family.description: B.Sc Nursing study companion for community health, maternal and newborn nursing, child health and mental health nursing — vital-statistics numericals, IMNCI-style triage, emergency scenarios and ticket labs. INC subject names are topic tags only; always follow national programme guidelines and your institution's protocols. A study companion only: it does not replace supervised clinical training or a licence.

courses.title: Community Health Nursing: Epidemiology, Immunisation & Home Visits
courses.summary: Vital statistics, India's Universal Immunisation Programme basics, cold chain, home visiting and health education in the community.
outcomes: Learners can calculate key vital statistics (IMR, MMR, CBR)
Learners can describe the UIP schedule basics
Learners can plan and conduct a home visit
Learners can manage an adverse event following immunisation

scenes.text: A sub-centre area recorded 1,250 live births and 35 infant deaths last year.
Calculate the infant mortality rate.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Key indicators
steps.body:
- **Crude birth rate** = live births ÷ mid-year population × 1,000
- **Infant mortality rate (IMR)** = deaths under 1 year ÷ live births × 1,000
- **Neonatal mortality rate** = deaths in first 28 days ÷ live births × 1,000
- **Maternal mortality ratio (MMR)** = maternal deaths ÷ live births × 100,000

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using total population as IMR denominator; mixing ratio (per 100,000 live births) and rate.

activity.prompt: A district had 40,000 live births and 52 maternal deaths. Maternal mortality ratio (per 100,000 live births)?

scenes.text: An ANM runs a village immunisation session.
Which vaccines are due?

steps.title: UIP highlights (check the current national schedule)
steps.body:
- **At birth:** BCG, OPV-0, Hepatitis B birth dose.
- **6, 10, 14 weeks:** OPV, pentavalent (DPT-HepB-Hib), rotavirus, fractional IPV (selected visits), PCV (as per schedule).
- **9–12 months:** measles–rubella (MR) first dose, (JE in endemic districts), vitamin A first dose.
- **16–24 months:** MR second dose, DPT booster, OPV booster.
- Further boosters (DPT at 5–6 years, Td at 10 and 16 years) and Td for pregnant women.

steps.title: Missed doses
steps.body: Do not restart a series — continue from where it stopped, respecting minimum intervals.

steps.title: Contraindications are few
steps.body: A mild cold or low-grade fever is not a reason to delay vaccination; true contraindications include anaphylaxis to a previous dose; live vaccines need caution in severe immunosuppression.

activity.prompt: Order the UIP visits

events.text: BCG, OPV-0, Hep B birth dose

options: Diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B, Hib
Not a reason to delay vaccination

scenes.text: You visit a mother 3 days after home delivery.
Plan and conduct the visit.

steps.title: Home visit principles
steps.body: Purposeful and planned; respect family culture; use the bag technique (hand hygiene, clean/dirty areas, newspaper lining); assess mother (bleeding, fever, breasts, mood, BP) and newborn (feeding, warmth, cord, jaundice, danger signs); educate; refer; record.

steps.title: Newborn danger signs
steps.body: Not feeding well, convulsions, fast breathing (≥60/min), severe chest indrawing, temperature ≥37.5 °C or <35.5 °C, lethargy/unconscious, yellow palms/soles, umbilical redness/pus → urgent referral.

steps.title: Breastfeeding
steps.body: Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, starting within the first hour after birth.

activity.prompt: Postnatal home visit checklist
items: Mother: bleeding, fever, BP, breasts, perineum, mood
Newborn: feeding, temperature, breathing, cord, skin colour
Counsel on family planning and immunisation
Refer urgently if danger signs; record the visit

quiz.q: Yellow palms and soles in a newborn suggest…

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — AEFI at the session

scenes.text: Ten minutes after vaccination, a 6-week-old becomes pale and unresponsive with difficulty breathing.
Respond.

steps.title: AEFI basics
steps.body: Minor: fever, local pain/swelling — reassure, paracetamol per guidance for fever if advised. Serious: anaphylaxis (within minutes, rash, breathing difficulty, hypotension), seizures, hypotonic–hyporesponsive episode → emergency management and referral; **report** through the AEFI surveillance system.

steps.title: Anaphylaxis at a session
steps.body: Call for help/112, lie the baby flat (or comfortable if breathing difficulty), IM adrenaline per the AEFI kit protocol, ABC support, transfer to the nearest facility. Keep vaccinees for 30 minutes after vaccination.

steps.title: Records
steps.body: Document vaccine, batch number, time, symptoms and actions; preserve vials as required for investigation.

a.text: Infant pale, unresponsive, wheezy 10 min after vaccination. First?

choices.label: Call for help, ABC, give IM adrenaline per AEFI kit protocol
Wait to see if it settles
Transfer to facility, document batch/time, report AEFI
Back

end1.text: Infant recovers in hospital; AEFI committee investigates.

options: Diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B, Hib
Not a reason to delay vaccination

questions.q: Yellow palms and soles in a newborn suggest…

courses.title: Maternal & Newborn Nursing: Antenatal to Postnatal
courses.summary: Antenatal assessment and EDD, danger signs in pregnancy, labour stages and partograph basics, postpartum haemorrhage response and newborn care.
outcomes: Learners can calculate EDD and gestational age
Learners can recognise danger signs in pregnancy
Learners can describe labour stages and AMTSL
Learners can respond to postpartum haemorrhage

scenes.text: A woman's last menstrual period (LMP) began on 10 March.
Calculate the EDD.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Naegele's rule
steps.body: EDD = LMP + 7 days − 3 months (+ 1 year), assuming a regular 28-day cycle. Example: LMP 10 March → **17 December**. Early ultrasound dating (first trimester) is more accurate and is used when it differs significantly.

steps.title: Gestational age
steps.body: Days since LMP ÷ 7. 196 days → **28 weeks**. Term pregnancy is 37–42 weeks (37+0 to 41+6 often defined as term).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding 7 days and 9 months but forgetting month-length differences; using LMP in irregular cycles without ultrasound.

activity.prompt: It has been 238 days since the first day of the LMP. Gestational age in completed weeks?

quiz.q: LMP 1 January → EDD by Naegele's rule:
Naegele's rule assumes a cycle of…

scenes.text: A 34-week pregnant woman reports severe headache and blurred vision; BP 160/110.
Recognise and refer.

steps.title: Danger signs
steps.body: Vaginal bleeding, severe headache/blurred vision/epigastric pain (pre-eclampsia), convulsions (eclampsia), high fever, severe abdominal pain, reduced/absent fetal movements, leaking fluid (rupture of membranes) before labour, severe breathlessness, swelling of face/hands.

steps.title: Pre-eclampsia
steps.body: New hypertension (≥140/90) after 20 weeks with proteinuria or organ involvement. Severe features → urgent obstetric care; magnesium sulfate is used to prevent/treat eclamptic seizures (per protocol, with monitoring of reflexes, RR and urine output; calcium gluconate as antidote).

steps.title: Refer
steps.body: Any danger sign → urgent referral to a facility with emergency obstetric care; call 112/ambulance (108 in many states).

activity.prompt: Danger sign or common minor discomfort?

items.text: Mild ankle swelling at day's end, normal BP

quiz.q: BP 160/110 with headache at 34 weeks suggests…
Drug used to prevent eclamptic seizures:

scenes.text: A primigravida is admitted in active labour.
Follow labour through its stages.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body:
**First stage:** onset of regular contractions to full dilatation (latent and active phases; monitor with partograph/WHO Labour Care Guide — contractions, FHR, cervical dilatation, descent, maternal vitals).
**Second stage:** full dilatation to birth of baby.
**Third stage:** birth of baby to delivery of placenta.
**Fourth stage:** first hour or so after placenta — close monitoring for PPH.

steps.title: AMTSL
steps.body: Active management of the third stage: **uterotonic (oxytocin 10 IU IM is the WHO-recommended drug)** within a minute of birth, controlled cord traction (by trained provider), uterine massage/tone checks after placenta. Delayed cord clamping (1–3 min) for the newborn if not needing resuscitation.

steps.title: Normal FHR
steps.body: Fetal heart rate about 110–160 bpm.

activity.prompt: Order the stages and key actions
items: First stage: monitor contractions, FHR, dilatation on partograph
Second stage: full dilatation to birth
Give oxytocin within 1 minute of birth (AMTSL)
Delayed cord clamping if baby is well
Controlled cord traction and delivery of placenta
Fourth stage: monitor uterine tone and bleeding

quiz.q: Third stage of labour ends with…

scenes.text: Fifteen minutes after a normal birth, a mother is bleeding heavily; the uterus feels soft.
Respond as a team.

steps.title: PPH
steps.body: Commonly defined as blood loss ≥500 mL after vaginal birth (≥1000 mL severe). Causes — **4 Ts**: Tone (atony, commonest), Trauma (tears), Tissue (retained placenta), Thrombin (clotting problems).

steps.title: First response (team, per protocol)
steps.body: Call for help, uterine massage, uterotonic per protocol, IV access with fluids, empty bladder, check placenta completeness and tears, monitor vitals and blood loss, tranexamic acid within 3 hours of birth per protocol, prepare for referral/transfusion.

steps.title: Shock signs
steps.body: Rising pulse, falling BP, pallor, confusion → escalate immediately.

choices.label: Call for help and massage the uterus
Wait 30 minutes to see if it stops
Give uterotonic per protocol, IV access and fluids, empty bladder, monitor

c.text: Uterus firm now, but still trickling; placenta complete. Consider?

choices.label: Check for genital tract trauma (tears) and repair/refer
Discharge
Back

end1.text: A cervical tear is repaired; she stabilises and is monitored closely.

Tranexamic acid in PPH is given…

courses.title: Child Health Nursing: Growth, Dehydration & Danger Signs
courses.summary: Growth monitoring, IMNCI-style danger signs, dehydration assessment and ORS/zinc, fever care and paediatric safety.
outcomes: Learners can plot and interpret growth
Learners can classify dehydration and plan ORS
Learners can recognise general danger signs
Learners can counsel caregivers on home care

scenes.text: A 2-year-old's weight has stayed flat for 3 months.
Use growth charts.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Charts
steps.body: WHO growth standards: weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, weight-for-height, MUAC. **Stunting** = low height-for-age (chronic); **wasting** = low weight-for-height (acute); **underweight** = low weight-for-age. Severe acute malnutrition in 6–59 months: weight-for-height < −3 SD, or MUAC <115 mm, or bilateral pitting oedema.

steps.title: Trend matters
steps.body: A flattening or falling curve is a warning even if still 'in the normal range'.

steps.title: Refer
steps.body: SAM with complications (poor appetite, illness, oedema) needs facility-based care (e.g. Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre).

activity.prompt: Match the indicator to its meaning

quiz.q: MUAC cut-off for SAM in 6–59 months:
A flat weight curve over months means…
SAM with complications should be managed…

scenes.text: A 14-month-old with diarrhoea: restless, irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, skin pinch goes back slowly.
Classify and plan.

steps.title: IMNCI-style classification
steps.body:
- **Severe dehydration** (≥2 of): lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, not able to drink or drinking poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly → Plan C (IV fluids/urgent referral).
- **Some dehydration** (≥2 of): restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly/thirsty, skin pinch goes back slowly → Plan B (ORS ~75 mL/kg over 4 hours in facility).
- **No dehydration** → Plan A (home fluids, ORS after each stool, continue feeding).

steps.title: Zinc and ORS
steps.body: Low-osmolarity ORS + **zinc for 10–14 days** (10 mg/day under 6 months; 20 mg/day 6 months and older) per national guidelines; continue breastfeeding.

steps.title: Plan B volume
steps.body: 12 kg child: 75 × 12 = **900 mL** ORS over 4 hours.

activity.prompt: Plan B for an 8 kg child with some dehydration: ORS volume over 4 hours at 75 mL/kg?

quiz.q: Restless, sunken eyes, thirsty, slow skin pinch →
Zinc for childhood diarrhoea is given for…

options: Home fluids, ORS after stools, continue feeding

quiz.q: ORS for 10 kg child in Plan B:

scenes.text: A busy paediatric OPD queue.
Pick out the children who cannot wait.

steps.title: General danger signs (2 months–5 years)
steps.body: Unable to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions (now or during this illness), lethargic or unconscious. Any one → urgent treatment and referral. Also emergency: obstructed breathing, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis, signs of shock, severe dehydration.

steps.title: Fast breathing thresholds
steps.body: 2–12 months ≥50/min; 12 months–5 years ≥40/min (counted for a full minute with the child calm).

steps.title: Fever
steps.body: Fever in a young infant (<2 months) or with danger signs, stiff neck or non-blanching rash → urgent referral.

activity.prompt: Urgent (see now) or can wait in queue?

quiz.q: Which is a general danger sign?
A non-blanching rash with fever needs…

scenes.text: A mother takes her child home on Plan A.
Counsel her clearly.

steps.title: Counselling
steps.body: Prepare ORS correctly (one packet in the stated volume of clean water, use within 24 h), give after each loose stool (under 2 years: 50–100 mL; 2 years and older: 100–200 mL), continue breastfeeding and food, give zinc daily for the full course, hand-washing with soap, safe water.

steps.title: When to return immediately
steps.body: Child becomes sicker, cannot drink or breastfeed, blood in stool, drinking poorly, fever develops, or danger signs.

steps.title: Teach-back
steps.body: Ask the mother to show how she'll mix the ORS.

activity.prompt: Plan A counselling checklist
items: Show how to mix ORS correctly
Explain how much to give after each stool
Give zinc daily for full course
Hand-washing with soap and safe water

Under 2 years, after each loose stool give about…

options: Blood in stool or unable to drink

courses.title: Mental Health Nursing: Communication, Risk & Safe Care
courses.summary: Therapeutic communication, mental status examination, suicide risk assessment and safety planning, de-escalation, psychotropic monitoring and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 in general terms.
outcomes: Learners can use therapeutic communication techniques
Learners can perform a basic mental status examination
Learners can assess suicide risk and escalate
Learners can monitor psychotropic side effects such as lithium toxicity

scenes.text: A newly admitted patient with depression sits silently and avoids eye contact.
Build rapport.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body: Active listening, open-ended questions ('Tell me about…'), reflecting feelings, paraphrasing, clarifying, using silence, summarising, offering self ('I'll sit with you for a while'). Non-therapeutic: false reassurance ('Everything will be fine'), giving advice too early, judging, changing the subject, 'why' questions that sound accusatory.

steps.title: Boundaries
steps.body: Warm but professional; no personal relationships or gifts; maintain confidentiality within the care team.

steps.title: Stigma
steps.body: Use person-first, respectful language ('a person living with schizophrenia').

activity.prompt: Therapeutic or non-therapeutic?

items.text: 'You seem sad today. Would you like to talk about it?'
'Why did you do such a silly thing?'
'So you're saying you feel nobody listens?'
'If I were you, I'd just go home.'

quiz.q: 'Everything will be fine' is an example of…
Repeating the patient's feeling back is…

scenes.text: You document a patient's mental state at admission.
Use the MSE structure.

steps.title: MSE headings
steps.body: **Appearance & behaviour** (grooming, eye contact, psychomotor activity) · **Speech** (rate, volume, tone) · **Mood** (subjective, in patient's words) and **affect** (observed; range, congruence) · **Thought form** (e.g. flight of ideas, loosening of associations) · **Thought content** (delusions, obsessions, suicidal/homicidal ideation) · **Perception** (hallucinations) · **Cognition** (orientation, attention, memory) · **Insight and judgement**.

steps.title: Quote the patient
steps.body: Record mood in the patient's own words: 'I feel empty'.

steps.title: Always ask about risk
steps.body: Suicidal thoughts, self-harm, harm to others, vulnerability — every MSE.

activity.prompt: Match the finding to the MSE heading
pairs: Hearing voices when no one is there
Accepts he is unwell and needs treatment

quiz.q: A fixed false belief is a…
Flight of ideas is a disorder of…

story.title: 'I don't see the point any more'

scenes.text: A patient tells you quietly she has been thinking she'd be better off dead.
Respond safely.

steps.title: Respond
steps.body: Asking directly about suicide **does not** increase risk. Ask about thoughts, plans, means, intent, previous attempts, protective factors. Do not leave a high-risk person alone; remove means; inform the team immediately; observation level per policy; collaborative safety plan.

steps.title: Risk factors
steps.body: Previous attempt (strongest), hopelessness, depression, substance use, recent loss, chronic illness/pain, social isolation, access to means. Protective: family support, reasons for living, engagement in care.

steps.title: Help numbers (India)
steps.body: Tele-MANAS **14416** (24×7 mental health support); emergency **112**.

a.text: Patient says she'd be better off dead. Your response?

choices.label: Thank her for telling you, ask directly about thoughts and plans
Change the subject to cheer her up

b.text: She has a plan and has been saving tablets. Next?

choices.label: Stay with her, remove means, inform the team immediately, follow observation policy
Promise to keep it secret

x.text: Ask directly — it is safe and essential.

choices.label: Back

end1.text: Team reviews urgently; close observation and a safety plan are put in place.

quiz.q: If a patient discloses a suicide plan, you should…
options: Not keep it secret; inform the team

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — psychotropic monitoring and rights

scenes.text: A patient on lithium has had vomiting and diarrhoea for two days and now has coarse tremor and unsteadiness.
Recognise toxicity.

steps.title: Lithium
steps.body: Narrow therapeutic index; levels monitored per protocol (typically 12 h post-dose). Toxicity is precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides. Signs: coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, ataxia, confusion, slurred speech, seizures → withhold per protocol and escalate urgently.

steps.title: Antipsychotics
steps.body: Monitor extrapyramidal effects (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), metabolic effects (weight, glucose, lipids), and **neuroleptic malignant syndrome** (fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability — emergency). Clozapine: neutropenia/agranulocytosis risk — regular blood counts.

steps.title: Rights (general)
steps.body: India's **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** emphasises rights to care, dignity, confidentiality, informed consent, advance directives and nominated representatives, and decriminalised attempted suicide by presuming severe stress. This is general education, not legal advice.

ticket.short: Patient shaky and unsteady after 2 days of D&V
ticket.description: Patient says 'my hands won't stop shaking and I feel drunk'. Vomited twice today. Has been taking ibuprofen for headache that a visitor brought.
worknotes: Last lithium level 3 weeks ago in range

investigate.label: Check observations and hydration
investigate.reveal: HR 104, BP 102/64, dry mucosa, reduced urine output.

investigate.label: Review medication history
investigate.reveal: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 3 days (not prescribed).

investigate.label: Check the patient's meal preferences
investigate.reveal: Vegetarian; not relevant to the acute problem.

investigate.label: Neurological check
investigate.reveal: Coarse tremor, ataxic gait, slightly confused.

options: Lithium toxicity precipitated by dehydration and NSAID
diagnosis.why: Coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion with D&V and NSAID use.

resolution: Escalate urgently to the doctor using SBAR
Withhold the next lithium dose per protocol/orders
Stop the unprescribed NSAID and inform the team
Obtain urgent lithium level, renal function and electrolytes as ordered
Start fluids as prescribed and monitor intake/output and neuro observations

closure.model: Suspected lithium toxicity (coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion) precipitated by 2 days of vomiting/diarrhoea and unprescribed ibuprofen. Escalated via SBAR; lithium withheld per order, NSAID stopped, urgent level 1.9 mmol/L, renal function checked, IV fluids given with neuro obs. Symptoms improved over 48 h; psychiatry and pharmacy reviewed regimen; visitor medicines policy reinforced.

uni-nursing-core.description: B.Sc Nursing study companion for fundamentals, safe medication and drug calculations, medical-surgical nursing and core procedures as step-by-step labs, with verified numericals and escalation scenarios. INC subject names are topic tags only; always follow your hospital's policies. A study companion only: it does not replace supervised clinical training or a licence.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Nursing: Vital Signs, Infection Control & Safety
courses.summary: Nursing process, vital signs and early-warning recognition, hand hygiene and infection prevention, patient safety and documentation.
outcomes: Learners can apply the nursing process (ADPIE)
Learners can measure and interpret vital signs
Learners can perform WHO hand hygiene at the right moments
Learners can document and hand over using SBAR

scenes.text: Mrs Das, 68, is admitted with breathlessness.
You plan her care using a structured process.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: ADPIE
steps.body: **Assessment** (subjective and objective data) → **Diagnosis** (nursing diagnosis, e.g. 'Impaired gas exchange related to… as evidenced by…') → **Planning** (SMART goals, priorities — ABC, Maslow) → **Implementation** → **Evaluation** (goals met? revise).

steps.title: Example nursing diagnosis
steps.body: Problem: Ineffective airway clearance · Related to: thick secretions · As evidenced by: productive cough, crackles, SpO₂ 91% on air. Goal: SpO₂ ≥ the target set by the medical team within 24 h; patient demonstrates effective coughing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing a medical diagnosis ('pneumonia') as the nursing diagnosis; goals without measurable criteria.

activity.prompt: Order the nursing process

quiz.q: The first step of the nursing process is…

options: The patient's response to health problems

lessons.title: Lab: Vital signs and early warning

scenes.text: At 2 a.m. a post-op patient is 'just sleepy'. RR 26, HR 118, BP 92/58, SpO₂ 92%, temperature 38.4 °C.
Is this an emergency?

steps.title: Adult normal ranges (approximate)
steps.body:
- Respiratory rate 12–20/min
- Heart rate 60–100/min
- Systolic BP ~100–139 mmHg (individual baseline matters)
- SpO₂ ≥95% in most adults on air (targets differ, e.g. 88–92% in some COPD patients as prescribed)
- Temperature 36.1–37.8 °C (approx.)
- Level of consciousness: ACVPU (Alert, new Confusion, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive)

steps.title: Early warning scores
steps.body: Systems such as NEWS2 add points for abnormal RR, SpO₂, BP, HR, consciousness and temperature; rising scores trigger escalation. **Respiratory rate** is the most sensitive early sign of deterioration and is often missed.

steps.title: Escalate
steps.body: New confusion, RR >24, systolic <90, HR >130, SpO₂ falling → escalate immediately per hospital protocol (rapid response team); suspect sepsis with infection signs.

activity.prompt: Normal or needs escalation? (adult, no special targets)

quiz.q: Most sensitive early sign of deterioration:

scenes.text: An infection-control audit is today.
Show the WHO technique and the 5 moments.

steps.title: WHO 5 Moments
steps.body:
1) Before touching a patient 2) Before a clean/aseptic procedure 3) After body fluid exposure risk 4) After touching a patient 5) After touching patient surroundings.

Alcohol-based hand rub 20–30 s; soap and water 40–60 s — use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled or for *C. difficile*/norovirus.

steps.title: PPE order
steps.body: Donning: hand hygiene → gown → mask/respirator → eye protection → gloves. Doffing (common sequence): gloves → hand hygiene → eye protection → gown → mask → hand hygiene. Follow your hospital's protocol.

steps.title: Gloves
steps.body: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene; change between patients and between dirty and clean tasks on the same patient.

activity.prompt: Order PPE donning
items: Put on gloves over gown cuffs

quiz.q: Alcohol hand rub should last about…
Use soap and water instead of rub for…
options: C. difficile or visibly soiled hands

scenes.text: Your post-op patient's NEWS score has risen.
Call the doctor using SBAR.

steps.title: SBAR
steps.body: **Situation:** who you are, patient, what's wrong now. **Background:** diagnosis, surgery, relevant history. **Assessment:** vital signs, your concern. **Recommendation:** what you need (review within X minutes, orders).

steps.title: Read-back
steps.body: Repeat back verbal orders and document them with time; follow your hospital's verbal-order policy.

steps.title: Documentation
steps.body: Document time, findings, who was called, advice received and actions — 'if it isn't documented, it wasn't done'.

activity.prompt: Put this SBAR call in order
items: S: 'I'm Nurse Anita on Ward 4; I'm calling about Mr Khan, bed 12, who is now breathless and hypotensive.'
B: 'He is day 1 after bowel surgery, history of diabetes.'
A: 'RR 26, HR 118, BP 92/58, SpO₂ 92%, temp 38.4 — NEWS high; I'm worried about sepsis.'
R: 'Please review him within 15 minutes; can I take blood cultures and start oxygen per protocol?'

quiz.q: In SBAR, vital signs and your concern go under…

options: Written later from memory without time
Time, findings, who was called, actions

options: The patient's response to health problems

lessons.title: Lab: Rights of medication and tablet calculations

scenes.text: Order: 500 mg; stock: 250 mg tablets.
How many tablets — and what must you check first?

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Rights
steps.body: Right patient (two identifiers), right drug, right dose, right route, right time, right documentation — plus right reason, right response, right to refuse. Check allergies; do three checks against the chart.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**Dose = (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity.**
500 mg ÷ 250 mg × 1 tablet = **2 tablets**.
Liquid: ordered 125 mg; stock 250 mg/5 mL → 125 ÷ 250 × 5 = **2.5 mL**.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: If a calculation gives an unusual number of tablets (e.g. >2–3) or a tiny/huge volume, stop and recheck with a colleague and the prescriber.

activity.prompt: Ordered: 0.25 mg. Stock: 0.125 mg tablets. How many tablets?

quiz.q: Ordered 750 mg; stock 250 mg/5 mL. Volume?

A patient has the right to…

scenes.text: Order: 40 mg IV; vial: 80 mg in 2 mL.
Calculate the volume to draw up.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
40 ÷ 80 × 2 = **1 mL**.
Heparin: order 5,000 units; vial 25,000 units/5 mL → 5,000 ÷ 25,000 × 5 = **1 mL**.
Concentration from %: 1% lidocaine = 10 mg/mL.

steps.title: Reconstitution
steps.body: Follow the product leaflet: add the stated diluent volume; note the displacement value (powder volume) — final concentration may differ from diluent volume.

steps.title: High-alert medicines
steps.body: Insulin, heparin, potassium chloride concentrates, opioids — independent double-check; never use abbreviations like 'U' for units (misread as 0).

activity.prompt: Order: 75 mg IM. Stock: 100 mg in 2 mL. Volume to draw up (mL)?

quiz.q: Writing 'U' for units is discouraged because…

lessons.title: Lab: IV flow and drip rates

scenes.text: Order: 1000 mL normal saline over 8 hours; giving set 20 drops/mL; no pump available.
Calculate mL/h and drops/min.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
**mL/h = volume (mL) ÷ time (h)** → 1000 ÷ 8 = **125 mL/h**.
**Drops/min = volume (mL) × drop factor (gtt/mL) ÷ time (min)** → 1000 × 20 ÷ 480 = 41.7 ≈ **42 drops/min**.

Common drop factors: macro sets 15 or 20 gtt/mL (check packaging); micro (paediatric) set 60 gtt/mL — then drops/min = mL/h.

steps.title: Check the time
steps.body: Mark the bag with time strips and check hourly; recalculate if behind schedule only per policy — never 'catch up' by large boluses.

steps.title: Paediatric/fluid-sensitive patients
steps.body: Use an infusion pump or burette for children, heart failure and renal patients.

activity.prompt: 500 mL over 4 hours with a 15 gtt/mL set. Drops per minute (round to nearest whole number)?

quiz.q: With a 60 gtt/mL microdrip set, drops/min equals…

options: Be reviewed per policy, not bolused to catch up

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — weight-based doses and infusions

scenes.text: A 22 kg child is prescribed 15 mg/kg every 6 hours of a medicine available as 250 mg/5 mL.
Check the dose before giving it.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1) 15 × 22 = 330 mg; volume = 330 ÷ 250 × 5 = **6.6 mL**.
2) Infusion in mcg/kg/min: 5 mcg/kg/min for a 70 kg adult; concentration 400 mg in 250 mL (1,600 mcg/mL) → mcg/min = 350; mL/h = 350 × 60 ÷ 1,600 = **13.1 mL/h**.

steps.title: Daily maximum
steps.body: Check single and 24-hour maximums in the formulary/label; question any dose outside them.

steps.title: Reminder
steps.body: These are training calculations. Real doses are prescribed by clinicians and verified per hospital policy.

options: Weight and 60, then dividing by concentration

courses.title: Medical-Surgical Nursing: Peri-operative, Diabetes & Cardiac Care
courses.summary: Pre- and post-operative care, pain and wound management, diabetes nursing including hypoglycaemia, and nursing care in chest pain and heart failure.
outcomes: Learners can prepare a patient for surgery
Learners can monitor post-op complications
Learners can manage hypoglycaemia per protocol
Learners can recognise and escalate chest pain

scenes.text: Mr Rao is listed for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Complete the pre-op checklist.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Pre-op essentials
steps.body: Identity band and allergy band; consent signed and valid; site marked where applicable; fasting per anaesthetic instructions (commonly no food ~6 h, clear fluids until ~2 h — follow local policy); medication instructions (e.g. anticoagulants, diabetes medicines); jewellery/dentures/prostheses removed; investigations available; VTE risk assessment; baseline vitals; voiding.

steps.title: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
steps.body: Sign in (before anaesthesia), Time out (before incision), Sign out (before leaving theatre).

steps.title: Stop
steps.body: Missing consent, unclear site, or unexpected abnormal vitals → inform the surgical/anaesthetic team before transfer.

activity.prompt: Pre-operative checklist
items: Two identifiers match the ID band
Allergies recorded and allergy band on

quiz.q: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist phases are…
options: Sign in, Time out, Sign out
Inform the team; do not proceed

quiz.q: Dentures are removed before anaesthesia because…

scenes.text: Your patient's wound drain shows fresh blood; HR rising; BP falling; restless.
Recognise and act.

steps.title: Complications to watch
steps.body:
- **Haemorrhage/hypovolaemic shock:** tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, restlessness, low urine output, increased drain/wound loss.
- **Respiratory:** atelectasis, pneumonia — encourage deep breathing, early mobilisation.
- **VTE:** calf pain/swelling; sudden breathlessness (PE).
- **Urinary retention**, **paralytic ileus**, **wound infection**, **post-op nausea and vomiting**, **delirium** in elderly.

steps.title: Urine output
steps.body: Adult target often ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; e.g. 70 kg → ≥35 mL/h.

steps.title: Escalate
steps.body: Signs of shock → call for help/rapid response, ABCDE, apply pressure to obvious bleeding, prepare IV access and fluids per orders.

activity.prompt: Match the sign to the complication

items.text: Rising pulse, falling BP, fresh drain blood
Sudden breathlessness and chest pain on day 4
No urine for 8 h, suprapubic discomfort

quiz.q: Minimum urine output for a 60 kg adult (0.5 mL/kg/h) is…
Sudden breathlessness after surgery may be…
Early sign of hypovolaemia is often…

scenes.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes on insulin is sweaty and confused; capillary glucose 3.1 mmol/L (56 mg/dL).
Act per protocol.

steps.title: Recognition
steps.body: Hypoglycaemia commonly defined as blood glucose <4.0 mmol/L (~70 mg/dL). Symptoms: sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, confusion, behaviour change, seizures, unconsciousness.

steps.title: Typical protocol (follow your hospital's)
steps.body: Conscious and able to swallow: 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate (e.g. glucose tablets or juice) → recheck in 10–15 min → repeat up to ~3 times → once >4 mmol/L give a long-acting carbohydrate snack. Unconscious/unable to swallow: call for help, nothing by mouth, IV glucose or IM glucagon per orders. Investigate the cause; do not omit future insulin without review.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for a conscious hypoglycaemic adult
items: Give a long-acting carbohydrate once recovered
Document and inform the medical team; review the cause

options: Not be given anything by mouth; IV glucose/IM glucagon per orders

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — chest pain on the ward

scenes.text: A 62-year-old in your ward develops central crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm, sweating.
Act fast.

steps.title: Immediate nursing actions
steps.body: Call for help/rapid response, stay with the patient, ABCDE, 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, vital signs and SpO₂, oxygen only if hypoxic per protocol, IV access, medications as prescribed/protocol (e.g. aspirin, GTN), keep nil by mouth, prepare for transfer to cardiac care, reassure.

steps.title: Heart failure nursing
steps.body: Daily weights (same time, scale, clothing), fluid balance, upright positioning when breathless, monitor for oedema; report weight gain of ~2 kg over 2–3 days.

steps.title: Cardiac arrest
steps.body: Unresponsive, not breathing normally → call arrest team, start CPR 30:2, attach defibrillator/AED.

a.text: Central chest pain with sweating. First?

choices.label: Call for help and do ABCDE; get ECG within 10 min
Give an antacid and reassess in an hour
choices.feedback: Dangerous delay — treat as possible ACS.

b.text: ECG shows ST elevation. SpO₂ 97%. Next?

choices.label: Inform team urgently; give prescribed protocol meds; prepare for reperfusion transfer
Give high-flow oxygen to everyone
choices.feedback: Oxygen only if hypoxic per guidelines.

choices.label: Back

end1.text: He is transferred for primary PCI within the target time and recovers.

courses.title: Core Nursing Procedures: Step-by-step Checklists
courses.summary: Evidence-based step sequences for injections, urinary catheterisation, nasogastric tube care, wound dressing and blood transfusion checks.
outcomes: Learners can sequence an IM injection safely
Learners can perform aseptic urinary catheterisation steps
Learners can confirm NG tube position safely
Learners can perform bedside blood transfusion checks

scenes.text: You give an IM injection to an adult in the deltoid.
Follow the safe sequence.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Key points
steps.body: Sites: deltoid (small volumes, adults commonly up to ~1 mL), ventrogluteal (preferred for larger volumes; avoids sciatic nerve), vastus lateralis (infants). Needle at 90°. Aspiration is not required for most vaccines per current guidance; follow local policy for other drugs. Z-track technique for irritant drugs.

steps.title: Sharps
steps.body: Never recap used needles; dispose immediately into a sharps container. Needlestick → wash, report, follow post-exposure protocol.

steps.title: Patient comfort
steps.body: Relax the muscle, insert quickly, inject slowly.

activity.prompt: Order the IM injection steps
items: Perform hand hygiene and prepare the medication
Clean skin per policy and allow to dry
Withdraw and dispose of sharps immediately

quiz.q: Preferred IM site for larger volumes in adults:

options: Not be recapped; go straight into sharps bin

scenes.text: A post-op patient has painful urinary retention; catheterisation is ordered.
Maintain asepsis to prevent CAUTI.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body: Confirm indication and order; consent and privacy; smallest appropriate catheter size; aseptic non-touch technique; sterile lubricant/anaesthetic gel; inflate balloon only after urine flows; closed drainage system below bladder level; document size, batch, volume drained, balloon volume.

steps.title: CAUTI prevention
steps.body: Remove catheters as soon as no longer needed; never let the bag rest on the floor or above bladder level.

steps.title: Male vs female
steps.body: Follow your institution's technique for each; never force against resistance — stop and escalate.

activity.prompt: Order the catheterisation steps
items: Insert lubricated catheter with non-touch technique
Wait for urine flow, then inflate balloon
Connect to closed drainage below bladder
Document size, volume drained and balloon volume

quiz.q: A key CAUTI prevention step is…
options: Remove catheter when no longer needed

scenes.text: A patient has a new nasogastric tube for feeding.
Confirm placement before anything goes down it.

steps.title: Safe confirmation
steps.body: Measure NEX (nose–ear–xiphisternum) length before insertion; after insertion aspirate and test with **pH indicator strip: pH ≤5.5** generally supports gastric placement (per many national policies). If no aspirate or pH >5.5 → do not use; chest X-ray interpreted by a competent clinician. **Never use the 'whoosh' (air auscultation) test, litmus paper or 'bubbling under water'** — they are unreliable.

steps.title: Each time
steps.body: Check position before every feed/medication, after vomiting/coughing, or if the external length mark has moved.

steps.title: Never event
steps.body: Feeding through a misplaced tube into the lungs can be fatal.

activity.prompt: Safe confirmation method or unsafe?

items.text: Chest X-ray reviewed by competent clinician
Placing tube end under water to look for bubbles

options: Unreliable and should not be used

quiz.q: If pH is 6.5 and no X-ray yet…
options: Do not use the tube; escalate

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — blood transfusion bedside check

scenes.text: A unit of red cells arrives for Mrs Sen.
The bedside check is where many fatal errors are caught.

steps.title: Bedside check
steps.body: Two qualified staff (or per policy) at the bedside: positive patient identification (ask name and DOB; check ID band) matches the compatibility label and the prescription; blood group, unit number, expiry, special requirements (irradiated etc.); inspect bag for leaks/clots/discolouration; baseline observations (temperature, pulse, BP, RR) before starting; repeat observations ~15 minutes after start and per policy; complete within the time limit (red cells usually within 4 hours of removal from storage).

steps.title: Transfusion reaction
steps.body: Fever, rigors, breathlessness, chest/loin pain, hypotension, rash → **stop the transfusion**, keep IV line open with saline (new line per policy), call doctor, monitor, return the bag and documents to the blood bank.

steps.title: Document
steps.body: Unit number, start/stop times, observations and staff signatures.

items: Positive patient ID at bedside (name, DOB, ID band)
Match ID band, compatibility label and unit details
Check expiry and inspect the bag
Repeat observations at ~15 minutes and per policy
Document unit number, times and signatures
